summary: Defines the Bearer authentication scheme for SIP and a way to delegate user authentication and registration authorization to a third party, using OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect Core 1.0. It also updates RFC 3261 with guidance on how a client responds to a 401 or 407 with multiple authentication header fields. It is standards-track.

eli5.summary: Instead of giving a phone service your password, you show a ticket from a trusted company that vouches for you. This document lets internet phone systems accept such tickets.

questions: how to use oauth with sip
what is the sip bearer authentication scheme
what is the authz_server parameter in sip
why must sip access tokens be encrypted
subtitle: How a SIP phone can prove who it is with an OAuth access token from a third party instead of a password.

tldr.problem: SIP authentication is a simple challenge-response between a client and a server. It gives no way to hand the sign-in step to a separate identity provider or to get single sign-on across SIP and non-SIP services.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8898 defines a "Bearer" authentication scheme for SIP. A server challenges with the address of an authorization server, the client gets an access token there using OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect, and then presents the token in the Authorization header of its SIP requests.
tldr.outcome: SIP servers can delegate user authentication and registration authorization to a third party. The document also updates RFC 3261 on how a client handles a 401 or 407 response with several challenges for the same realm.

today: RFC 8898 is a Proposed Standard, published in September 2020. It updates RFC 3261 and has not been obsoleted or updated by a later RFC.

sections.title: Delegating SIP Sign-In to a Third Party
sections.content:
The Session Initiation Protocol (SIP, RFC 3261) authenticates users the way HTTP does: a server challenges a request and the client answers the challenge. OAuth 2.0 (RFC 6749) is a token-based authorization framework, and OpenID Connect Core 1.0 adds an identity layer on top of it.

RFC 8898 defines the Bearer authentication scheme for SIP, so that user authentication and SIP registration authorization can be handed to a third party. This enables single sign-on: the user authenticates once and gains access to both SIP and non-SIP services.

The document only covers cases where the client can obtain an access token from the authorization server (AS) directly. Cases where it cannot, for example an authorization code grant, are not covered.
sections.eli5: Think of a theme park wristband. You prove who you are once at the gate, and then every ride just checks the wristband. Here the wristband is a token that many services can accept.

sections.title: Tokens and Their Formats
sections.content:
What the client receives depends on the kind of server it talks to. An OAuth authorization server gives a successfully authorized client an access token, which the client shows to a SIP server to gain access to services, and may also give a refresh token, which the client presents to the AS to renew a stale access token. An OpenID Provider (OP) returns one more token, the ID token, which holds a SIP URI associated with the user and other user details for the client to consume.

Tokens come in two formats. A structured token is an object carrying its own claims, such as a JSON Web Token (JWT, RFC 7519). A reference token is an opaque string used to look up the token's details and claims. Access tokens can be either. Refresh tokens are usually reference tokens, because only the issuing AS consumes them. The ID token is defined as a JWT.
sections.eli5: A structured token is a ticket with everything printed on it. A reference token is a ticket with just a number, and you have to call the office to learn what it allows.

sections.title: The Registration Flow
sections.content:
In the main example, a client sends a REGISTER request with no credentials. The registrar answers 401 Unauthorized with a WWW-Authenticate: Bearer header that names the authorization server in an authz_server parameter. The client then talks to the AS using a mechanism that is out of scope here, possibly the OAuth native app approach in RFC 8252, which sends the user to a web browser so the AS can ask for multi-factor authentication or redirect to other identity providers.

The client retries the REGISTER with an Authorization: Bearer header carrying the access token. The registrar validates it. If it is a reference token, the registrar MAY use token introspection (RFC 7662) to learn more about the token and its scope. Otherwise it inspects the claims itself. On success it replies 200 OK.

If the client is preconfigured with the AS, it can fetch tokens first and skip the challenge round trip.
sections.eli5: You knock on the door with no ticket, and the doorman tells you which ticket office to visit. You get a ticket there, come back, and the doorman lets you in.

sections.title: Client, Server and Proxy Behavior
sections.content:
The procedures of RFC 3261 for Digest authentication also apply to Bearer, with changes. When a client gets a 401 or 407 that offers Bearer and an AS address, it contacts the AS, asking for the scopes its local configuration calls for. It MUST check the AS URL against a list of trusted authorization servers configured on the client, to prevent several classes of vulnerabilities when a client blindly uses any AS it is told about. If the client holds a refresh token it uses it to get a new access token before the old one expires. Otherwise it must reauthenticate the user.

For a REGISTER, the client sends the token in an Authorization header as in RFC 6750. A new token is typically obtained for each new binding, but local policy MAY allow reusing a token from another binding for the same Address Of Record. For other requests, the client MUST include a Bearer token and MAY reuse one from another dialog if the target is the same.

A UAS or registrar that accepts tokens and chooses to challenge MUST send a WWW-Authenticate header with the Bearer scheme and an https URI for the AS. It MUST validate any presented token, and MUST reply 401 if the token is expired or validation fails. A proxy does the same with 407 and Proxy-Authenticate, and MUST validate the credentials from at least one Proxy-Authorization header for its realm.

If a 401 or 407 carries several challenges with different schemes for the same realm, the client answers one scheme it supports, chosen by local policy. The RFC notes that detailed procedures for this case had not been defined, and that a future specification might define them.
sections.eli5: The visitor must only go to ticket offices on an approved list, so a trickster cannot send them to a fake one. The doorman then checks every ticket and turns away old or fake ones.

sections.title: The Bearer Challenge Syntax
sections.content:
The document extends the SIP challenge grammar with a Bearer form. Each challenge can carry these parameters:

  • realm and auth-param, as defined by RFC 3261.
  • scope, a list of space-delimited, case-sensitive strings defined by the AS. The server uses it to tell the client the minimum scope the token needs.
  • authz_server, the https URI of the AS. The client can discover metadata about the AS with a mechanism like RFC 8414.
  • error, with possible values invalid_token or invalid_scope.

What the token grants is a matter of local policy agreed between the AS and the registrar. A JWT token carries claims the registrar can act on, while a reference token needs another mechanism such as introspection or a user profile lookup.
sections.eli5: The doorman's note has a few blanks to fill in: which ticket office to use, what kind of ticket is needed, and what went wrong if your last ticket was refused.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
TLS only protects SIP signaling hop by hop, and SIP uses intermediary proxies. So the access token MUST be protected so that only authorized SIP servers can read it. Endpoints that support this document MUST use encrypted JWTs for access tokens in SIP requests, unless another mechanism guarantees that only authorized SIP endpoints can see the token.

Single sign-on has a cost: if the login is compromised, the damage reaches every service that uses it. The RFC suggests a long passphrase, multi-factor authentication and the native platform browser. Both parties should let users sever the SSO relationship, and the operator of the SSO system can see which services their users log into, which should be stated in privacy disclosures.

A registrar that offers several service levels is RECOMMENDED to include a scope naming the minimum needed for basic services.
sections.eli5: A ticket passed from hand to hand could be copied, so it goes in a sealed envelope that only the right people can open. And since one wristband opens many doors, it must be guarded well.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: IANA is asked to add three header field parameters, authz_server, error and scope, to the SIP "Header Field Parameters and Parameter Values" registry. They are registered for both the Proxy-Authenticate and the WWW-Authenticate header fields. None has predefined values.
sections.eli5: The new words in the doorman's note are written in the official dictionary so everybody uses them the same way.
